acceptance_criteria.criterion: All five repositories use CommandDefinition for every Dapper call that accepts a CancellationToken.

summary: Replaced all bare QueryAsync/QuerySingleAsync/QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync/QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync/ExecuteAsync calls with new CommandDefinition(sql, param, [transaction:], cancellationToken: cancellationToken) in all 5 repository files.
DapperTagsRepository.cs: 25+ calls updated including transaction-aware calls in DeleteTagAsync (5 statements) and MergeTagAsync (9 statements).
DapperMovieRepository.cs: 8 calls updated across GetByIdAsync, SaveAsync, ResetViewCountAsync, SetReviewAsync, GetOriginalFilenameAsync, GetKnownActorNamesAsync, GetKnownStudiosAsync.
DapperMovieCatalogRepository.cs: 6 calls updated. DapperFilterSlotRepository.cs: 5 calls. SpdbConfigRepository.cs: 3 calls (2 transaction-aware).
Build: 0 errors, 0 warnings. All 583 tests pass.

comments.note: DapperTagsRepository.DeleteTagAsync and MergeTagAsync pass ownedTx (which may be null) as the transaction in CommandDefinition. CommandDefinition accepts null transaction without issue — this is correct and consistent with the existing pattern.

The LAST_INSERT_ID() calls use CommandDefinition with only a cancellationToken (no parameters). These are session-scoped MySQL functions and are safe in this context since each method uses a single connection per call. If connection pooling behaviour ever changes (e.g., connection multiplexing), the LAST_INSERT_ID pattern could return stale data — but this is pre-existing design, not introduced by this WP.

SpdbConfigRepository.IsSchemaPresentAsync is not on the ISpdbConfigRepository interface by design (documented in the inline comment). The CT sweep updates this method consistently even though it is not polymorphically accessible — no change needed.
